pathway.title: CoreWeave, Inc. — Credit Snapshot
pathway.question: Should we own this issuer, in which instrument, and why?

runs.text: First, leverage is high and rising faster than earnings. CoreWeave had principal debt of USD 35,551 million at June 30, 2026 against USD 21,615 million at December 31, 2025, and LTM adjusted EBITDA of USD 4,400 million, giving 8.08x gross and 6.82x net of unrestricted cash and marketable securities, against 6.99x and 5.97x at year end [Documentary Fact; financial base]. Cash interest cover on adjusted EBITDA is 3.35x, or 2.35x against net interest expense of USD 1,874 million. Both ratios flatter the position: adjusted EBITDA adds back stock compensation, cash interest is net of capitalized interest of USD 322 million over the twelve months, and on operating income plus depreciation and amortization gross leverage is 9.46x [Analyst Interpretation]. Mechanism: debt funds assets that are not yet earning, so period-end debt over trailing earnings overstates run-rate leverage, but operating income is already negative after interest-bearing growth, with an LTM operating loss of USD (231) million and the LTM net loss is USD (1,928) million.

Second, cash flow does not cover investment. Six months 2026 operating cash flow was USD 3,663 million against purchases of property and equipment of USD 14,117 million, leaving free cash flow of USD (10,454) million; the twelve-month figure is USD (13,655) million [Documentary Fact]. The gap is funded by new debt, equity placements of USD 2.0 billion (NVIDIA, January 2026) and USD 1.0 billion (April 2026), and customer prepayments, with deferred revenue at USD 9,692 million [Documentary Fact]. Implication: the credit relies on markets staying open; a funding pause would force a cut in capital spending and slow the delivery that converts backlog to revenue.

Third, liquidity is large on paper and conditional in practice. Company-reported total liquidity was USD 15,553 million at June 30, 2026: cash USD 5,524 million, marketable securities USD 15 million and availability USD 10,014 million, which rebuilds as USD 1,967 million on the revolver, USD 385 million on DDTL 3.0, USD 5,663 million on DDTL 4.0 and USD 1,999 million on DDTL 5.0 [Documentary Fact]. Draws on the delayed-draw facilities are limited to eligible asset purchases, the DDTL 3.0 and DDTL 5.0 draw periods ended before the as-of date, and restricted cash of USD 1,380 million sits outside the figure. In August 2026, after the quarter, CoreWeave drew USD 1.2 billion on the revolver and USD 1.2 billion on the new DDTL 5.5 facility, which lowers revolver availability (USD 767 million on the financial base's indicative basis) and means cash and availability at the as-of date are Not calculable [Analyst Interpretation].

Fourth, the maturity profile is front-loaded relative to cash. Scheduled principal is USD 4,413 million in the remainder of 2026, USD 6,184 million in 2027, USD 4,416 million in 2028, USD 2,421 million in 2029, USD 3,221 million in 2030 and USD 14,896 million after that; current debt is USD 7,513 million against cash of USD 5,524 million [Documentary Fact]. Much of the near-term amount is scheduled amortization on asset-level facilities and equipment financing, which is likely to be serviced from contracted cash flows rather than refinanced [Analyst Interpretation], but DDTL 4.0 payment timing is a management estimate. Implication: near-term refinancing risk is real but concentrated in amortizing secured debt; the unsecured and convertible notes mature from 2030 onward.

Fifth, revenue visibility is strong but concentrated and delivery-dependent. Committed contracts have a weighted-average duration of about five years, remaining performance obligations are USD 103.7 billion with 41% due within 24 months, and management cites a wider backlog of about USD 104 billion plus more than USD 25 billion of commitments added in early Q3 [Documentary Fact and Management Language, kept apart]. Three customers supplied 36%, 26% and 10% of Q2 2026 revenue (72% together), customers A and B were 32% each of receivables, and customer labels change between periods, so the fall from 71% for one customer a year earlier is not a like-for-like trend [Documentary Fact]. Mechanism: take-or-pay terms fix revenue, but revenue is recognized only as capacity is delivered (393 MW undelivered at one leased site), and service credits reduce the backlog. Implication: counterparty quality of a few customers drives default risk for the asset-level facilities.

Sixth, claims outside the debt figure are large. Operating lease liabilities are USD 16,319 million, finance leases USD 221 million, leases signed but not commenced USD 35.5 billion undiscounted, joint venture funding commitments up to USD 1.7 billion, and accrued purchases USD 5,520 million [Documentary Fact]. Debt plus lease liabilities would be USD 52,091 million; no lease-adjusted ratio is offered because adjusted EBITDA is stated after operating lease cost. Implication: fixed charges will rise as leases commence, ahead of the revenue they support.

Seventh, structure and control limit what a creditor can verify. About 89.5% of principal debt is recourse (USD 31,832 million) and USD 3,719 million is non-recourse; delayed-draw facilities are secured on subsidiary assets and guaranteed by the parent except DDTL 4.0, while the notes are unsecured and guaranteed by unnamed subsidiaries [Documentary Fact]. Founders hold all Class B shares, which carry about 66.9% of votes on the cover-page counts, and no sponsor is named [Analyst Interpretation]. Mechanism: asset-level lenders hold first-priority liens on the financed equipment and cash flows, so value available to unsecured holders depends on residual value after those claims; this is a mechanic, not a recovery conclusion. Material weaknesses in internal control continued at June 30, 2026 and securities suits are pending with no accrual.

runs.text: Strengths. CoreWeave has long contracted revenue: committed contracts are 98% of Q2 2026 revenue and remaining performance obligations are USD 103.7 billion with a weighted-average contract duration of about five years [Documentary Fact]. It has grown fast, with Q2 2026 revenue of USD 2,575 million against USD 1,212 million a year earlier, up 112.5%, and LTM revenue of USD 7,590 million [Documentary Fact]. It has shown access to several funding sources in 2026, including secured delayed-draw loans, unsecured notes, convertibles, a euro bond and two equity placements, which supports refinancing capacity while markets stay open [Analyst Interpretation]. Adjusted EBITDA margin was 58.0% over the last twelve months [Documentary Fact; management measure]. The asset-level structure ties each facility to financed assets and contracted cash flows, with the parent guaranteeing all but DDTL 4.0 [Documentary Fact]. Counterparties named in the sources include Microsoft, OpenAI, Meta and Jane Street, with commitments of up to about USD 6.5 billion, USD 21.0 billion and USD 6.0 billion for the last three [Documentary Fact].

Weaknesses. Leverage is high: 8.08x gross and 6.82x net on adjusted EBITDA, and 9.46x gross on operating income plus depreciation and amortization [Documentary Fact]. Free cash flow is deeply negative at USD (10,454) million for six months 2026, so the business consumes external capital [Documentary Fact]. Earnings after interest are negative: the LTM operating loss is USD (231) million and net interest expense USD 1,874 million [Documentary Fact]. Refinancing and amortization are near term, with USD 4,413 million and USD 6,184 million due in the remainder of 2026 and 2027 [Documentary Fact]. Customer concentration is high, with three customers at 72% of Q2 2026 revenue [Documentary Fact]. Off-balance-sheet lease commitments of USD 35.5 billion and joint venture commitments of up to USD 1.7 billion add to future fixed charges [Documentary Fact]. Control is with founders through a ten-vote share class and no sponsor support is documented [Analyst Interpretation]. Material weaknesses in internal control continue, which weakens the reliability of figures used in lender tests [Documentary Fact]. Stockholders' equity of USD 5,024 million is small against principal debt of USD 35,551 million [Documentary Fact]. Covenant levels, guarantors and financing documents are not supplied, so headroom and legal protections cannot be tested [Insufficient Information].

blocks.title: Transaction summary and new debt issues

runs.text: There is no merger, buyout or sponsor transaction in the sources. The transaction content is a financing programme, set out in date order with status as of the filing of the Q2 2026 quarterly report, and the figures match the financial base handoff. In January 2026 NVIDIA bought about 23 million Class A shares for 2.0 billion gross (completed). In March 2026 a subsidiary, CoreWeave Compute Acquisition Co. VIII, LLC, signed the DDTL 4.0 facility of 8.5 billion with MUFG Bank as administrative agent, available for draws to June 30, 2027 and maturing in March 2032 (10-Q 2026-06-30, pages:28-29); it is non-recourse apart from limited carve-out guarantees, is secured on the equity and substantially all assets of that subsidiary, and had 2,837 million outstanding at June 30, 2026 (CP-1). Floating loans bear SOFR plus 2.25% and fixed loans bear 2.00% over a Treasury-based rate. In April 2026 the company issued 2.8 billion of 9.75% senior notes due October 2031 (2,750 million principal) and 4.0 billion of 1.75% convertible senior notes due October 2032 (conversion price about 119.60, no redemption before October 8, 2029, capped calls costing 492 million with a cap price of 230.00); a portion of the convertible proceeds funded the capped calls, the remainder is for general corporate purposes, and the senior note proceeds were retained for general corporate purposes (10-Q 2026-06-30, pages:32-33). The revolver was repaid in April 2026 and convertible promissory notes of 172 million principal (168 million carrying at December 31, 2025) were settled in shares at 106.61 per share (pages:31 and 34). In May 2026 CoreWeave Financing DDTL V, LLC signed the DDTL 5.0 facility of 3.1 billion with Morgan Stanley as administrative agent at SOFR plus 4.50%, drawable to September 30, 2026, repayable monthly from November 2026, guaranteed by the parent and secured on subsidiary equity and assets, with 1,101 million outstanding at June 30, 2026 (page:30). In June 2026 the company issued 1.3 billion of 9.625% senior notes due July 2032 and 2.0 billion euro of 8.50% senior notes due July 2032, hedged with a cross currency swap, with proceeds retained for general corporate purposes (pages:19 and 33-34). Notes are unsecured and guaranteed by certain wholly-owned subsidiaries (page:134). The financing is part of a layered structure: recourse parent debt, parent-guaranteed single-purpose facilities, and non-recourse debt; liquidity effect was cash of 5,524 million at June 30, 2026 against 2,244 million at March 31, 2026 (CP-1). After the quarter, in August 2026, the company signed the DDTL 5.5 facility of 2.6 billion with JPMorgan as agent at SOFR plus 5.5%, maturing September 2031, drawable to December 2026, and drew 1.2 billion; it also drew 1.2 billion on the revolver (page:46). Uses: delayed draw facilities finance computing equipment purchases, subject to debt-sizing limits tied to the cost of eligible assets; notes and convertibles fund general corporate purposes. Status of each: completed and drawn, except undrawn commitments (DDTL 4.0, DDTL 5.0 and DDTL 5.5 balances), which depend on eligible asset purchases. Off-balance-sheet lease and joint venture commitments (35.5 billion of leases not yet commenced, 1.7 billion of joint venture funding) sit alongside the debt and are in the financial base handoff. Conflicts and limits: the DDTL 5.0 maturity is printed as November 2031 in the debt table and as an expected final payment in May 2031 in the text, logged below and not reconciled; the sources do not contain the indentures or credit agreements, so use-of-proceeds restrictions, guarantor lists and covenants are Not supplied.

fields.value: The financial base is sufficient to describe the June 30, 2026 position and the path from FY2025, with stated limits. The audited FY2025 statements, three quarterly filings and three releases tie to each other: six months 2026 revenue of $4,653 million equals Q1 2026 plus Q2 2026, and the debt table sums to the printed total. The picture is of fast, debt-financed growth. Revenue in Q2 2026 was $2,575 million against $1,212 million a year earlier, adjusted EBITDA was $1,510 million, but the company still reported an operating loss of $(49) million and net interest expense of $(640) million in the quarter. Principal debt of $35,551 million (about 89.5 percent recourse by principal, calculated below) is mostly secured, project-level delayed-draw debt plus unsecured notes and convertibles. Leverage on LTM adjusted EBITDA is 8.08x gross and 6.82x net of unrestricted cash and marketable securities, and cash interest cover is 3.35x; both are flattered by the EBITDA definition (it adds back stock compensation and acquisition costs, and is struck after operating lease cost, so lease cost is not in the add-backs) and by cash interest being net of capitalized interest. Debt at period end also funds assets not yet earning revenue, so period-end debt over trailing earnings overstates run-rate leverage, and the contracted backlog (remaining performance obligations of $103.7 billion) is the offsetting evidence. The main restrictions are that financial covenant levels are not printed, so headroom is Not calculable, that guarantors are not named, and that nothing after the Q2 2026 filing except the August 2026 events in the filing note is in the pack.

fields.value: CoreWeave sells GPU-based AI cloud capacity, mostly through multi-year take-or-pay contracts, and finances the equipment and data center build-out with asset-level debt backed by those contracts, supplemented by corporate notes, convertibles and equity. The evidence supports a creditor view built on three mechanics. First, revenue visibility is long: committed contracts have a weighted-average duration of about five years, and the filing reports a large contracted backlog, but that backlog converts to revenue only as capacity is delivered and made available, and the filings disclose power still undelivered at leased sites. Second, concentration is the main operating risk: a handful of customers account for most revenue, named customers include Microsoft, OpenAI, Meta and Jane Street, and the identity of the top customers changes between filings. Third, funding is the main structural risk: each growth step is paid for by new debt or equity, and the debt mixes recourse parent obligations, parent-guaranteed subsidiary facilities and one non-recourse facility, so the claim a creditor holds depends on which entity borrowed and who guaranteed. Ownership is public with founders holding control through a ten-vote share class; no sponsor is named, and no ownership percentages are disclosed in the sources read. Documented issuer behaviour is mostly supportive (equity issued alongside debt) and otherwise neutral; no dividend recapitalization, priming or uptier is documented in the pages read, but the executed documents that would show what is permitted are not supplied. Management claims in releases (power, backlog, partnerships) are attributed and not adopted.

fields.value: There is no merger, buyout or sponsor transaction in the sources. The transaction content is a financing programme, set out in date order with status as of the filing of the Q2 2026 quarterly report, and the figures match the financial base handoff. In January 2026 NVIDIA bought about 23 million Class A shares for 2.0 billion gross (completed). In March 2026 a subsidiary, CoreWeave Compute Acquisition Co. VIII, LLC, signed the DDTL 4.0 facility of 8.5 billion with MUFG Bank as administrative agent, available for draws to June 30, 2027 and maturing in March 2032 (10-Q 2026-06-30, pages:28-29); it is non-recourse apart from limited carve-out guarantees, is secured on the equity and substantially all assets of that subsidiary, and had 2,837 million outstanding at June 30, 2026 (CP-1). Floating loans bear SOFR plus 2.25% and fixed loans bear 2.00% over a Treasury-based rate. In April 2026 the company issued 2.8 billion of 9.75% senior notes due October 2031 (2,750 million principal) and 4.0 billion of 1.75% convertible senior notes due October 2032 (conversion price about 119.60, no redemption before October 8, 2029, capped calls costing 492 million with a cap price of 230.00); a portion of the convertible proceeds funded the capped calls, the remainder is for general corporate purposes, and the senior note proceeds were retained for general corporate purposes (10-Q 2026-06-30, pages:32-33). The revolver was repaid in April 2026 and convertible promissory notes of 172 million principal (168 million carrying at December 31, 2025) were settled in shares at 106.61 per share (pages:31 and 34). In May 2026 CoreWeave Financing DDTL V, LLC signed the DDTL 5.0 facility of 3.1 billion with Morgan Stanley as administrative agent at SOFR plus 4.50%, drawable to September 30, 2026, repayable monthly from November 2026, guaranteed by the parent and secured on subsidiary equity and assets, with 1,101 million outstanding at June 30, 2026 (page:30). In June 2026 the company issued 1.3 billion of 9.625% senior notes due July 2032 and 2.0 billion euro of 8.50% senior notes due July 2032, hedged with a cross currency swap, with proceeds retained for general corporate purposes (pages:19 and 33-34). Notes are unsecured and guaranteed by certain wholly-owned subsidiaries (page:134). The financing is part of a layered structure: recourse parent debt, parent-guaranteed single-purpose facilities, and non-recourse debt; liquidity effect was cash of 5,524 million at June 30, 2026 against 2,244 million at March 31, 2026 (CP-1). After the quarter, in August 2026, the company signed the DDTL 5.5 facility of 2.6 billion with JPMorgan as agent at SOFR plus 5.5%, maturing September 2031, drawable to December 2026, and drew 1.2 billion; it also drew 1.2 billion on the revolver (page:46). Uses: delayed draw facilities finance computing equipment purchases, subject to debt-sizing limits tied to the cost of eligible assets; notes and convertibles fund general corporate purposes. Status of each: completed and drawn, except undrawn commitments (DDTL 4.0, DDTL 5.0 and DDTL 5.5 balances), which depend on eligible asset purchases. Off-balance-sheet lease and joint venture commitments (35.5 billion of leases not yet commenced, 1.7 billion of joint venture funding) sit alongside the debt and are in the financial base handoff. fields.value: CoreWeave, Inc. is a high-risk credit: its contracted demand is strong, but its balance sheet depends on continued access to new debt and equity. The strongest support is revenue visibility, with committed contracts at 98% of Q2 2026 revenue and remaining performance obligations of USD 103.7 billion. The weakest point is financial: principal debt of USD 35,551 million at June 30, 2026 is 8.08x LTM adjusted EBITDA, and six months 2026 free cash flow was USD (10,454) million. The outcome will be decided by delivery and funding: whether CoreWeave brings contracted capacity online on time, collects from a concentrated customer base, and refinances USD 4,413 million due in the remainder of 2026 and USD 6,184 million in 2027 while delayed-draw commitments stay conditional.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: First, leverage is high and rising faster than earnings. CoreWeave had principal debt of USD 35,551 million at June 30, 2026 against USD 21,615 million at December 31, 2025, and LTM adjusted EBITDA of USD 4,400 million, giving 8.08x gross and 6.82x net of unrestricted cash and marketable securities, against 6.99x and 5.97x at year end [Documentary Fact; financial base]. Cash interest cover on adjusted EBITDA is 3.35x, or 2.35x against net interest expense of USD 1,874 million. Both ratios flatter the position: adjusted EBITDA adds back stock compensation, cash interest is net of capitalized interest of USD 322 million over the twelve months, and on operating income plus depreciation and amortization gross leverage is 9.46x [Analyst Interpretation]. Mechanism: debt funds assets that are not yet earning, so period-end debt over trailing earnings overstates run-rate leverage, but operating income is already negative after interest-bearing growth, with an LTM operating loss of USD (231) million and the LTM net loss is USD (1,928) million.

fields.value: Second, cash flow does not cover investment. Six months 2026 operating cash flow was USD 3,663 million against purchases of property and equipment of USD 14,117 million, leaving free cash flow of USD (10,454) million; the twelve-month figure is USD (13,655) million [Documentary Fact]. The gap is funded by new debt, equity placements of USD 2.0 billion (NVIDIA, January 2026) and USD 1.0 billion (April 2026), and customer prepayments, with deferred revenue at USD 9,692 million [Documentary Fact]. Implication: the credit relies on markets staying open; a funding pause would force a cut in capital spending and slow the delivery that converts backlog to revenue.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: Third, liquidity is large on paper and conditional in practice. Company-reported total liquidity was USD 15,553 million at June 30, 2026: cash USD 5,524 million, marketable securities USD 15 million and availability USD 10,014 million, which rebuilds as USD 1,967 million on the revolver, USD 385 million on DDTL 3.0, USD 5,663 million on DDTL 4.0 and USD 1,999 million on DDTL 5.0 [Documentary Fact]. Draws on the delayed-draw facilities are limited to eligible asset purchases, the DDTL 3.0 and DDTL 5.0 draw periods ended before the as-of date, and restricted cash of USD 1,380 million sits outside the figure. In August 2026, after the quarter, CoreWeave drew USD 1.2 billion on the revolver and USD 1.2 billion on the new DDTL 5.5 facility, which lowers revolver availability (USD 767 million on the financial base's indicative basis) and means cash and availability at the as-of date are Not calculable [Analyst Interpretation].

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: Fourth, the maturity profile is front-loaded relative to cash. Scheduled principal is USD 4,413 million in the remainder of 2026, USD 6,184 million in 2027, USD 4,416 million in 2028, USD 2,421 million in 2029, USD 3,221 million in 2030 and USD 14,896 million after that; current debt is USD 7,513 million against cash of USD 5,524 million [Documentary Fact]. Much of the near-term amount is scheduled amortization on asset-level facilities and equipment financing, which is likely to be serviced from contracted cash flows rather than refinanced [Analyst Interpretation], but DDTL 4.0 payment timing is a management estimate. Implication: near-term refinancing risk is real but concentrated in amortizing secured debt; the unsecured and convertible notes mature from 2030 onward.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: Fifth, revenue visibility is strong but concentrated and delivery-dependent. Committed contracts have a weighted-average duration of about five years, remaining performance obligations are USD 103.7 billion with 41% due within 24 months, and management cites a wider backlog of about USD 104 billion plus more than USD 25 billion of commitments added in early Q3 [Documentary Fact and Management Language, kept apart]. Three customers supplied 36%, 26% and 10% of Q2 2026 revenue (72% together), customers A and B were 32% each of receivables, and customer labels change between periods, so the fall from 71% for one customer a year earlier is not a like-for-like trend [Documentary Fact]. Mechanism: take-or-pay terms fix revenue, but revenue is recognized only as capacity is delivered (393 MW undelivered at one leased site), and service credits reduce the backlog. Implication: counterparty quality of a few customers drives default risk for the asset-level facilities.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: Sixth, claims outside the debt figure are large. Operating lease liabilities are USD 16,319 million, finance leases USD 221 million, leases signed but not commenced USD 35.5 billion undiscounted, joint venture funding commitments up to USD 1.7 billion, and accrued purchases USD 5,520 million [Documentary Fact]. Debt plus lease liabilities would be USD 52,091 million; no lease-adjusted ratio is offered because adjusted EBITDA is stated after operating lease cost. Implication: fixed charges will rise as leases commence, ahead of the revenue they support.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: Seventh, structure and control limit what a creditor can verify. About 89.5% of principal debt is recourse (USD 31,832 million) and USD 3,719 million is non-recourse; delayed-draw facilities are secured on subsidiary assets and guaranteed by the parent except DDTL 4.0, while the notes are unsecured and guaranteed by unnamed subsidiaries [Documentary Fact]. Founders hold all Class B shares, which carry about 66.9% of votes on the cover-page counts, and no sponsor is named [Analyst Interpretation]. Mechanism: asset-level lenders hold first-priority liens on the financed equipment and cash flows, so value available to unsecured holders depends on residual value after those claims; this is a mechanic, not a recovery conclusion. Material weaknesses in internal control continued at June 30, 2026 and securities suits are pending with no accrual.

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: Strengths. CoreWeave has long contracted revenue: committed contracts are 98% of Q2 2026 revenue and remaining performance obligations are USD 103.7 billion with a weighted-average contract duration of about five years [Documentary Fact]. It has grown fast, with Q2 2026 revenue of USD 2,575 million against USD 1,212 million a year earlier, up 112.5%, and LTM revenue of USD 7,590 million [Documentary Fact]. It has shown access to several funding sources in 2026, including secured delayed-draw loans, unsecured notes, convertibles, a euro bond and two equity placements, which supports refinancing capacity while markets stay open [Analyst Interpretation]. Adjusted EBITDA margin was 58.0% over the last twelve months [Documentary Fact; management measure]. The asset-level structure ties each facility to financed assets and contracted cash flows, with the parent guaranteeing all but DDTL 4.0 [Documentary Fact]. Counterparties named in the sources include Microsoft, OpenAI, Meta and Jane Street, with commitments of up to about USD 6.5 billion, USD 21.0 billion and USD 6.0 billion for the last three [Documentary Fact].

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: Weaknesses. Leverage is high: 8.08x gross and 6.82x net on adjusted EBITDA, and 9.46x gross on operating income plus depreciation and amortization [Documentary Fact]. Free cash flow is deeply negative at USD (10,454) million for six months 2026, so the business consumes external capital [Documentary Fact]. Earnings after interest are negative: the LTM operating loss is USD (231) million and net interest expense USD 1,874 million [Documentary Fact]. Refinancing and amortization are near term, with USD 4,413 million and USD 6,184 million due in the remainder of 2026 and 2027 [Documentary Fact]. Customer concentration is high, with three customers at 72% of Q2 2026 revenue [Documentary Fact]. Off-balance-sheet lease commitments of USD 35.5 billion and joint venture commitments of up to USD 1.7 billion add to future fixed charges [Documentary Fact]. Control is with founders through a ten-vote share class and no sponsor support is documented [Analyst Interpretation]. Material weaknesses in internal control continue, which weakens the reliability of figures used in lender tests [Documentary Fact]. Stockholders' equity of USD 5,024 million is small against principal debt of USD 35,551 million [Documentary Fact]. Covenant levels, guarantors and financing documents are not supplied, so headroom and legal protections cannot be tested [Insufficient Information].

fields.name: Quote
fields.value: Credit thesis: CoreWeave's long, contracted, take-or-pay revenue supports a fast-growing asset-level financing model, but the heavy debt load, negative free cash flow and customer concentration make the credit dependent on on-time delivery and continued access to capital.
